name: THE NO KIMCHI FOR OLD MEN BURGER

recipe.history:
Kimchi is one of the oldest and most complex fermented foods in human history, with evidence of vegetable fermentation on the Korean peninsula dating back over three thousand years. The earliest kimchi was not the fiery red preparation we know today — chili peppers, now inseparable from kimchi's identity, were not introduced to Korea until Portuguese traders brought them from the Americas in the sixteenth century. Before that, kimchi was made with vegetables preserved in brine, sometimes with garlic and ginger, sometimes with soybean paste, in the tradition of fermented preservation that allowed communities to survive harsh Korean winters. After the introduction of chili, the dish transformed rapidly, and by the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, baechu-kimchi — the napa cabbage kimchi that is now the canonical version — had developed into the form still made today. Kimchi-making, known as kimjang, is a collective cultural practice in which communities gather each autumn to prepare enormous quantities for the winter months, and in 2013, UNESCO recognized kimjang as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. There are over two hundred documented varieties of kimchi in Korea, ranging from mild water kimchi to intensely fermented, pungent preparations aged for months or years.

Kimchi arrived in America primarily through Korean immigration following the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which opened the United States to significant Korean immigration for the first time. Korean restaurants in cities like Los Angeles, New York, and Chicago introduced kimchi to American diners, where it was initially regarded as an acquired taste — fermented, pungent, spicy, and aggressively flavored in ways that American palates conditioned on milder pickled products were not accustomed to. The Los Angeles Korean food truck scene of the late 2000s, epitomized by the Kogi Truck, was a watershed moment: it showed that kimchi belonged on a taco, a quesadilla, a burger — that fermented Korean funk was not merely compatible with American comfort food but actively improved it. Since then, kimchi has become a fixture in upscale burger culture, appearing in multiple preparations: raw as a topping, cooked into butter as a condiment, blended into mayonnaise as a sauce. Aged kimchi, with its deeper, more sour, more complex fermented character, elevates all these applications.

I started fermenting my own kimchi after a cook I worked with in a restaurant kitchen showed me how her grandmother's recipe differed from every jar she had tried in a store. The homemade version was alive in a way that commercial kimchi rarely is — still actively fermenting, the brine fizzing faintly when you stirred it, the cabbage crunchy and the heat blooming slowly rather than hitting all at once. She made a batch every few weeks and kept jars at different stages of fermentation in a small cooler under her prep station. The young kimchi she put on grilled meats raw. The older kimchi, weeks into its fermentation, she cooked into butter and spread on bread. The oldest kimchi, months old and deeply sour, she simmered into soups and stews. I learned from her that kimchi is not one ingredient but a spectrum, and this burger is built on that lesson: every preparation is a different age, a different face of the same fundamental thing.

Medium rare at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit is not a point on a temperature scale — it is a philosophy of restraint. Kimchi brings enormous assertiveness to a burger: the fermented funk, the chili heat, the garlic sharpness, the acid of the brine. The only thing that can hold its own against all of that without being swamped is a patty that is still juicy, still rich, still full of rendered fat and pink meat. A well-done patty is a white flag — it has surrendered all its moisture and character to the heat and can no longer compete with the kimchi's intensity. The result is a burger where the topping dominates and the meat disappears, which is the opposite of what a great burger should be. Cook to medium rare, pull at 130 to 135, rest properly, and you will have a patty that pushes back against the kimchi, creating the dynamic tension that makes every bite interesting.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 tbsp toasted sesame seeds for topping
1 tbsp fish sauce (or soy sauce for vegetarian)
Note: For this recipe, use well-fermented kimchi aged at least 3 to 4 weeks; store-bought aged kimchi is acceptable.
4 tbsp unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
3 tbsp finely minced aged kimchi (squeezed very dry)
4 slices sharp cheddar or American cheese
1 tsp toasted sesame seeds for garnish
instructions: 1. Make the kimchi (if making from scratch, begin 3 to 4 weeks ahead): Quarter the napa cabbage lengthwise and cut into 2-inch pieces. Toss with kosher salt in a large bowl. Let sit 1 to 2 hours, tossing occasionally, until the cabbage wilts and releases liquid. Rinse thoroughly under cold water, then drain and squeeze as dry as possible.

2. Combine minced garlic, grated ginger, gochugaru, fish sauce, and sugar in a large bowl. Add the drained cabbage and scallions. Mix thoroughly with gloved hands, coating every piece. Pack tightly into clean glass jars, pressing down firmly to eliminate air pockets. Leave 1 inch of headspace. Seal loosely and let ferment at room temperature 1 to 2 days until slightly bubbly, then refrigerate. Use after 3 to 4 weeks for full aged character.

3. Make the kimchi butter: Combine softened butter, minced aged kimchi, kimchi brine, sesame oil, and sugar in a small bowl. Mix vigorously until completely combined and uniform. Form into a log in plastic wrap and refrigerate until firm. Slice into pats before use.
4. Make the kimchi mayo: Stir together mayonnaise, minced kimchi, kimchi brine, gochujang, rice wine vinegar, and sesame oil until fully combined. Refrigerate until needed.

5. Make the sesame brioche buns: Combine warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Add flour one cup at a time with the dough hook on low until a shaggy dough forms. Increase to medium speed, add butter cube by cube, and mix 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight.

6. Divide dough into 4 equal portions, shape into tight balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover loosely and proof at room temperature 1.5 to 2 hours. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with toasted sesame seeds. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden brown. Cool on a wire rack.

7. Form the patties: Mix sesame oil gently into the ground beef. Divide into 4 portions and form into 4-inch patties, 3/4-inch thick, with a dimple in the center. Season both sides with salt and pepper. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat and lightly oil the surface. Sear patties dimple-side up for 3 minutes undisturbed. Flip once, place a pat of kimchi butter on each patty (let it melt over the top), and lay a slice of cheese on top. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes until internal temperature reaches 130 to 135°F. Remove from heat, tent loosely with foil, and rest 3 minutes.
9. In the same skillet over medium-high heat, add a splash of oil and sauté the roughly chopped aged kimchi for 3 to 4 minutes until slightly caramelized and fragrant. Remove and set aside.
10. Split the sesame brioche buns and toast cut-side down in the remaining kimchi butter in the skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

11. Assemble the burgers: Spread kimchi mayo generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place the rested patty on the bottom bun. Top with a mound of the sautéed aged kimchi. Scatter thinly sliced scallions and a pinch of toasted sesame seeds over the top. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately.
